title: India's Brutal Heatwave Has Killed 18 People. The Government's Answer? Sattu, Amla, and Ancient Ayurvedic Wisdom.
excerpt: As temperatures breach 47°C across North India and the death toll climbs, the Ministry of Ayush has issued an extraordinary advisory blending modern medicine with traditional Indian remedies — a move NRIs watching from abroad should take seriously.
body:
Madhya Pradesh recorded 47.5°C last week. Delhi is bracing for 45°C. At least 18 people have died across multiple states, and the India Meteorological Department warns the worst is not over. This is not a routine Indian summer — it is a heatwave of historic severity, and it has prompted an unusual intervention from New Delhi: a public health advisory from the Ministry of Ayush that reads less like a government circular and more like a grandmother's prescription.

## What the Advisory Actually Says

Issued jointly with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, the Ayush advisory is striking for how seriously it takes India's traditional medical systems. Alongside standard guidance — stay hydrated, avoid midday sun, watch for heatstroke symptoms — the document recommends specific Ayurvedic and Siddha practices: cooling foods to pacify what Ayurveda calls aggravated Pitta dosha, herbal preparations, and lifestyle adjustments rooted in millennia-old Indian medical texts.

The advisory highlights sattu (roasted gram flour drink) as a natural coolant and electrolyte replenisher. It recommends amla (Indian gooseberry) juice, coconut water, buttermilk, and aam panna (raw mango drink) — beverages that any Indian grandmother would recognise but that the Indian government is now officially endorsing as public health measures. Traditional practices like applying sandalwood paste, wearing loose cotton clothing, and adjusting meal timing to avoid heavy food during peak heat are also included.

For heatstroke, the advisory is unequivocal: it is a medical emergency requiring immediate hospital attention. But for prevention, it argues that India's ancient systems offer tested, accessible, and cost-effective solutions — particularly for the hundreds of millions who lack easy access to modern healthcare.

## The Numbers Behind the Crisis

The IMD has issued orange and red alerts across Northwest and Central India. Delhi's Safdarjung Observatory recorded 44.6°C on May 14, with five other stations exceeding 46°C. Rajasthan, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Haryana, Punjab, and Odisha are all affected. Schools across North and Central India have extended summer holidays. The central government has urged states to reschedule outdoor work hours, provide accessible water stations, and ensure ventilation for vulnerable workers in construction and brick kilns.

Climate data suggests this is no anomaly. El Niño years have been shown to reduce Kharif crop output by over 10 per cent across states, and IMD forecasts predict above-normal temperatures persisting through May. Vulnerable populations — infants, the elderly, pregnant women, outdoor labourers, and those with chronic conditions — face the greatest risk.

## Why NRIs Are Paying Attention

For the diaspora, India's heatwaves are no longer abstract headlines. Many NRIs have elderly parents, grandparents, or extended family in affected regions, and the anxiety is real. WhatsApp family groups across the US, UK, and Canada are buzzing with forwarded advisories, temperature screenshots, and urgent reminders to check on relatives.

The Ayush advisory carries a particular resonance for NRIs who grew up with these remedies. Sattu was what your nani made in Bihar summers. Aam panna was a fixture of Delhi childhoods. Buttermilk after lunch was not a health hack — it was just what you did. Seeing the Indian government validate these traditions as legitimate public health measures is quietly affirming, even as the crisis that prompted the advisory is deeply alarming.

There is also a practical dimension. NRIs planning summer trips to India — wedding season, family visits, temple pilgrimages — need to take the heatwave seriously. Travel insurance that covers heat-related illness, adjusting itineraries to avoid outdoor activities between 11 AM and 4 PM, and packing oral rehydration salts are now sensible precautions, not excessive ones.

## The Pitta Problem — Ayurveda's Framework for Heat

Ayurveda frames summer heat as an aggravation of Pitta dosha, one of three fundamental energies governing the body. When Pitta spikes, the body responds with inflammation, acidity, skin irritation, fatigue, and irritability. The Ayurvedic prescription is not to fight the heat but to cool the system: favour sweet, bitter, and astringent tastes over salty, sour, and pungent ones. Drink room-temperature water infused with mint or fennel seeds. Eat lighter meals. Avoid alcohol and caffeine.

These are not fringe claims. India's National Institute of Ayurveda and multiple peer-reviewed studies have documented the cooling and anti-inflammatory properties of many traditional Indian foods and herbs. The Ayush advisory's integration into a mainstream health communication is a signal that India's government is increasingly willing to position traditional medicine as complementary to, rather than in competition with, modern healthcare.

## What's Next

The heatwave is expected to persist for at least two more days, and the monsoon remains weeks away. For NRIs, the immediate action is simple: call your family, make sure they have access to water and shade, and take the advisory's recommendations seriously. For India, the deeper question is whether it can build the infrastructure — early warning systems, urban cooling centres, heat-resilient housing — to make these crises survivable without relying on the resilience of its poorest citizens. The sattu will help. The policy has to follow.
